# Epistle of Barnabas — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Anonymous (NOT the Barnabas of Acts — the attribution is a later claim) |
| **Date** | c. 70–135 CE (probably after the destruction of the Temple; possibly after 135 CE) |
| **Audience** | Gentile Christians, possibly in Alexandria or Syria |
| **Genre** | Theological letter / allegorical biblical commentary |
| **Timeline** | Early second century, in the aftermath of the Jewish-Roman wars |
| **In One Sentence** | A powerful and troubling early Christian text that reads the entire Hebrew Bible as a book about Jesus — arguing that Israel never properly understood its own scriptures — preserved in Codex Sinaiticus and nearly canonical. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

The Epistle of Barnabas was written in the shadow of catastrophe. Either the Temple has just been destroyed (70 CE) or the Second Jewish Revolt has just been crushed and Jerusalem obliterated (135 CE, after the Bar Kokhba revolt). In either case, the Jewish world has been shattered, and the author is interpreting that shattering theologically. His conclusion is stark: God had never truly accepted Israel's sacrifices, festivals, and circumcision as valid in the first place, because Israel misread the commandments by taking them literally when they were always meant spiritually and allegorically.

The community the author addresses is Gentile Christian. They do not practice Torah. They are not tempted to Judaize. The author's concern is apparently not that they will join the synagogue but that the ongoing existence of Jewish religious practice — even in its post-Temple, diaspora form — might confuse them about the meaning of the scriptures both communities share. He wants to ensure they understand that the Hebrew Bible belongs entirely to the church, not to Israel, because Israel had forfeited the covenant through idolatry with the golden calf before Moses even brought the tablets down from the mountain (chapter 4). This is not a footnote — for Barnabas, Israel never received the covenant at all.

This is theological reading from a position of Gentile confidence in the decades after the Jewish catastrophe, and it carries all the dangers of such a position: it reads the other's defeat as proof of their permanent displacement, it claims the other's sacred texts as one's own, and it does so without ever engaging seriously with the Jewish tradition's own reading of those texts. The author is not vicious or contemptuous in tone — he is earnest and pastoral — but the structural logic of his argument is supersessionism in its starkest early form.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The author's primary purpose is to establish that the covenant belongs entirely to the church — that Christians, not Jews, are the true inheritors of Abraham and Moses. He does this through a sustained allegorical reading of the Torah in which almost every commandment becomes a prophecy about Christ. The dietary laws (chapter 10) are not really about animals: the prohibition on eating swine means "do not consort with people who, when they are comfortable, forget the Lord, but when they are in need they remember him" (like swine, who grunt loudly when hungry and are silent when fed). The prohibition on eating rabbit means "do not become one who corrupts boys." Every prohibition maps onto a spiritual/ethical warning.

The famous "318 servants" passage (chapter 9) is the most celebrated example of this method. Genesis 14:14 records that Abraham took 318 trained men to rescue Lot. The author asks: why 318? In Greek, the numbers 10, 8, and 300 are represented by the letters iota (I), eta (H), and tau (T). Iota and eta spell "IH" — the first two letters of IHSOUS (Jesus in Greek). Tau (T) is the shape of the cross. Therefore, Abraham's 318 servants secretly encode the name of Jesus and the cross. This is not parody — it is dead serious allegorical typology, and it was enormously influential in establishing a method of reading that would dominate Christian biblical interpretation for centuries.

A secondary purpose is ethical formation: chapters 18–21 contain the Two Ways material (parallel to the Didache), providing a catechetical framework for the moral life. The letter is thus not purely theoretical — it has a practical dimension, ensuring that the congregation's allegorical reading of scripture issues in concrete ethical behavior.

---

## How to Read This Book

Read the Epistle of Barnabas in three movements.

The first movement (chapters 1–17) is the allegorical reading of Torah. Begin with chapter 2, where the author argues that God "abolished" the sacrificial system even in the Old Testament itself, citing Isaiah, Psalms, and Zechariah to show that God was always more interested in repentance and justice than in burnt offerings. This is not unique to Barnabas — it echoes the prophetic critique of sacrifice throughout the Hebrew Bible and appears in Stephen's speech in Acts 7 and in the Letter to the Hebrews. What is distinctive in Barnabas is the conclusion drawn: that the Torah was never meant to be observed literally.

Chapter 9 (circumcision = the 318 servants = Jesus and the cross) and chapter 10 (dietary laws as spiritual/ethical allegory) are the most important to read carefully. Note the method: it is not "here is what the text means in addition to its literal meaning" (typology), but "here is what the text actually means — the literal reading was always a mistake." This is a crucial distinction. Paul in Romans and Galatians uses the first approach; Barnabas uses the second.

Chapter 16 on the Temple is historically significant: the author argues that the Temple was never truly God's dwelling place (citing Isaiah 66:1 — "Heaven is my throne and earth my footstool; what house will you build for me?"), and that the true temple is the human heart indwelt by the Spirit. This passage may reflect awareness of the Temple's destruction.

The second movement (chapters 18–21) is the Two Ways. Read it alongside the Didache's version to see the similarities and differences. Barnabas's Two Ways is slightly shorter and placed at the end rather than the beginning, which suggests a different structural purpose — here it functions as a summary conclusion rather than an initial gate.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

The allegorical method of Barnabas connects most directly to the Alexandrian tradition of Jewish biblical interpretation, specifically to Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE–50 CE), whose massive allegorical commentaries on the Torah demonstrate that this approach to scripture was already well developed in Hellenistic Judaism before Christianity adopted it. The author of Barnabas may well have been Alexandrian, or at least educated in the Alexandrian tradition.

The Two Ways section connects directly to the Didache (chapters 1–6), with both texts apparently drawing on a common Jewish catechetical source. The parallel is close enough that scholars debate whether Barnabas or the Didache's version is earlier, or whether both are independent derivatives of a lost common source.

The Letter to the Hebrews (in the New Testament) shares Barnabas's interest in demonstrating that the Torah's cultic provisions pointed beyond themselves to Christ, but Hebrews does so through typology (the Levitical system was a "shadow" of the reality in Christ) rather than through Barnabas's stronger claim that the literal observance was always mistaken. Reading Hebrews and Barnabas together illuminates the spectrum of early Christian engagements with Torah.

The anti-Jewish hermeneutic of Barnabas connects to a trajectory that runs through Melito of Sardis's Peri Pascha (c. 170 CE), Tertullian's Against the Jews, John Chrysostom's Adversus Judaeos homilies, and ultimately to the long history of Christian theological anti-Judaism. The connection is not causal — Barnabas did not cause this history — but it is part of the same pattern of thought, and its presence in a near-canonical text is historically significant.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The most important thing to understand about Barnabas's method is that it is not dishonest — it is a genuine, earnest application of what the author believes is the correct way to read scripture. He did not know he was being supersessionist in a modern problematic sense. He was writing in a context of real crisis and genuine theological inquiry. But that does not absolve modern readers of the responsibility to see what the method does: it removes the Hebrew Bible from the hands of the community that produced it, denies that community any ongoing covenant standing, and uses their texts to argue against them.

Modern readers should also notice how much the author loves the Old Testament. He quotes it incessantly, with delight and energy. His point is not that the Hebrew Bible is obsolete — quite the opposite: it is endlessly full of Christ, secretly pointing to Jesus on every page. The problem, for him, is not the text but Israel's misreading of it. This is a love of scripture that has gone deeply wrong structurally.

The "318 servants" passage is worth understanding as a specimen of gematria — the practice of finding hidden meanings in numbers, a practice deeply embedded in both Jewish (the numerical value of Hebrew letters) and Greek (likewise for Greek letters) intellectual culture. This is not eccentric or marginal — it is a recognized method in the ancient world. The real question it raises is methodological: once you commit to this kind of reading, what prevents you from finding anything in anything?

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

Barnabas was included in Codex Sinaiticus — one of the two oldest complete New Testament manuscripts (the other being Codex Vaticanus), dated to the fourth century. Its presence in Sinaiticus shows that some communities treated it as canonical or near-canonical. Eusebius listed it among the "disputed" (antilegomena) books, acknowledging its reputation while noting its contested standing.

Its exclusion from the canon was not primarily due to its anti-Jewish hermeneutic (which was, sadly, not unusual for the period) but to doubts about apostolic authorship. The attribution to Barnabas, the companion of Paul in Acts, was questioned early. Origin noted the uncertainty. By the time Athanasius made his definitive 27-book list in 367 CE, Barnabas was excluded, though it retained high esteem in Alexandria.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Church's broader canon does not include Barnabas, but the text continued to be read and cited throughout the patristic period. Its discovery in Codex Sinaiticus in 1859 (by Constantin von Tischendorf at St. Catherine's Monastery, Sinai) gave it renewed scholarly attention. It is today recognized as a crucial — and deeply uncomfortable — witness to early Christian theological self-definition in relation to Judaism.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| 70 CE | Destruction of the Jerusalem Temple (possible background for the text) |
| c. 70–135 CE | Epistle of Barnabas composed (date debated) |
| 132–135 CE | Bar Kokhba revolt; Jerusalem refounded as Aelia Capitolina (possible terminus post quem) |
| c. 150–200 CE | Text circulating widely; Clement of Alexandria quotes it |
| c. 313 CE | Eusebius lists it as "disputed" |
| c. 350 CE | Included in Codex Sinaiticus |
| c. 367 CE | Athanasius excludes it from his canon |
| 1859 CE | Tischendorf discovers Codex Sinaiticus at St. Catherine's Monastery |
| 1844–1859 CE | Gradual publication of Sinaiticus text |
| 1900s–present | Recognized as significant but deeply problematic early Christian text |

---
